passage: I'm Ishita, and in second year I spent three hours convinced that the university's online judge was broken. My code for sorting names worked on my laptop. On the site, it failed every time. Lab instructor's note, electronics lab, second-year.
Wasim spent most of today's session insisting his multimeter was faulty because his circuit read zero volts. He borrowed two more meters and got the same result. He then told me the question sheet must have wrong values. I asked him to walk me through the circuit from the battery. He pointed to each part until he reached the switch, which was off. He had assumed it was on because the light on the board was glowing, but that light belonged to the power supply, not his circuit. His lab partner, Shalini, had asked him earlier if he'd checked the switch; he'd waved it away. Next week I will introduce a checklist: verify each assumption before blaming the tools.

qa.a: He borrowed two more meters.

qa.a: He felt frustrated and sure of his own setup, so blaming the tools felt more likely than an error of his.

qa.q: Why did walking through the circuit help?
qa.a: It made Wasim check each assumption step by step, until the switch he assumed was on turned out to be off.

qa.a: Shalini might feel a mix of vindication and mild annoyance, having asked about the switch earlier and been waved away.

Spent three hours convinced the survey form was broken. The average age of my respondents came out as 94. Obviously the form was scrambling the data. I wrote an angry message to the course helpdesk and told Sunaina the university's tools are a joke.
Sunaina, very calmly: "Did you look at the raw answers?"
No. Why would I? I built the form myself, I know what's in it.

Deleted the helpdesk message before sending it. Mildly mortified.
Note to self: check what I assumed before blaming the machine.
Ankita
